articles.title: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN: Which Rows Survive?
articles.description: Most JOIN confusion comes down to one question: what happens to rows with no match? Here's how INNER and LEFT JOIN answer it, and how to choose. Adapted from the SQL Essentials Companion Guide. Every explanation of SQL joins seems to reach for the same overlapping-circles diagram, and many people still come away unsure which join to use. It helps to drop the diagram and ask one plain question: what happens to a row that has no match in the other table? That single question is the whole difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. Everything else about them is the same. A tiny example Take two small tables. customers holds three people, and orders holds the purchases they made: customers orders id | name id | customer_id | amount ---+----- ---+-------------+------- 1 | Ada 10 | 1 | 50 2 | Ben 11 | 1 | 30 3 | Cy 12 | 2 | 20 13 | 99 | 70 Ada has two orders, Ben has one, and Cy has none. Order 13 points at customer 99, who doesn't exist. Two rows here have no match: Cy on one side, order 13 on the other. The joins differ in what they do with them. INNER JOIN keeps only the matches SELECT customers.name, orders.amount FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id; name | amount -----+------- Ada | 50 Ada | 30 Ben | 20 Only rows that found a partner appear. Cy is gone because Cy has no orders, and order 13 is gone because it has no customer. INNER JOIN drops anything without a match, on both sides. Writing JOIN on its own means the same thing. LEFT JOIN keeps everything from the left table LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id; Cy | NULL Now Cy is back, with NULL where the order columns would be. The "left" table is the one written before the JOIN keyword, here customers. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from that table, whether or not it found a match, and fills in NULL for the right table's columns when it didn't. Order 13 is still absent, because it lives in the right table and has no customer. So the choice comes down to this: if a row without a match should still show up in your results, use LEFT JOIN. If it should disappear, use INNER JOIN. A useful trick: finding what's missing Because LEFT JOIN fills in NULL for non-matches, you can use it to find rows that have no match at all. Filter for the NULL: SELECT customers.name WHERE orders.id IS NULL; name ---- Cy That's "customers who have never ordered." It's one of the most useful things a LEFT JOIN does, and the same pattern answers any "which X have no Y" question. Note that it uses IS NULL, not = NULL. If that distinction is new to you, Why 'WHERE x = NULL' Never Works in SQL explains it. How to practice choosing Before you write a join, say the result out loud: "I want every customer, and their orders if they have any" (that's LEFT), or "I want only customers who have orders" (that's INNER). The wording tells you which to use. Then run it on a small table where you know the answer, like the one above, and check that the row you expected to survive did. If you ever get stuck, count rows. Run SELECT COUNT(*) on the left table alone, then on the join. With an INNER JOIN, the join can come back with fewer rows than the left table, because unmatched rows disappeared. With a LEFT JOIN, every left row is still there, so you won't see fewer than the left table has. Two mistakes worth knowing about ahead of time Filtering the right table in WHERE and accidentally undoing your LEFT JOIN. This catches almost everyone once. Suppose you want all customers, plus only their orders over 25: WHERE orders.amount > 25; Ben and Cy vanished. For them, orders.amount is NULL after the join (Ben's only order is 20), and NULL > 25 is never true, so WHERE throws those rows out. You've turned your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN without noticing. To keep every customer, put the condition in the ON clause, so it limits which orders match instead of which rows survive: LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id AND orders.amount > 25; Ben | NULL Counting with COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN. COUNT(*) counts rows, and Cy's row exists even though there's no order, so Cy shows as 1. Count a column from the right table instead, such as COUNT(orders.id), which skips NULL and correctly gives Cy 0. And if a join ever returns more rows than you expected, the cause is a different one, covered in Why Your JOIN Doubled Your Totals. A habit that makes joins easy Treat LEFT JOIN as your starting point and INNER JOIN as a deliberate choice. Ask yourself first which table is the one you really care about, the one whose rows must not vanish, and put it on the left. Then decide whether unmatched rows belong in the answer. Doing it in that order turns a choice that feels like guesswork into two short questions, and it makes the "where did my rows go?" surprise much rarer. If you'd like more posts like this sent straight to your inbox, subscribe to the newsletter. Prefer to dig in yourself? The SQL Essentials repo on GitHub has more free examples and exercises.

articles.title: The Real Challenge in Agent Automation Isn't Intelligence — It's Not Crashing Mid-Workflow
articles.description: Today's GitHub Trending tells a clear story: agents are moving from single-step demos to long-running, multi-step execution. vercel-labs/agent-browser gives agents CLI control over browsers. ZhuLinsen/daily_stock_analysis runs a full pipeline — multi-source market data, real-time news, LLM analysis, dashboard, auto-push notifications — on a schedule. milind-soni/OpenMausBot gives bots their own virtual machine to execute in. These projects are impressive. But they all surface the same engineering problem that anyone who's actually deployed agent workflows knows intimately: When step 7 of a 10-step workflow fails, you lose everything. We learned this the hard way. We were running an agent pipeline that collected data from multiple sources, processed it through an LLM, generated a report, and pushed it to stakeholders. Steps 1 through 6 ran fine. Step 7 — an API call to a third-party service — timed out. The entire workflow crashed. When we restarted, it began from step 1. The model wasn't the problem. The orchestration layer was. Nobody had built checkpoint-based resume into the workflow. Nobody was persisting state between steps. Nobody was isolating failure so one broken step didn't poison the rest. What Long-Running Agent Workflows Actually Need After hitting that wall, we rebuilt our orchestration layer with three core capabilities: 1. Step-level checkpointing. Every step's output is persisted before the next step begins. If step 7 fails, the system knows exactly where to resume — with the full context of steps 1-6 intact. 2. Isolated retry with backoff. When a step fails, it retries in isolation. It doesn't trigger a full workflow restart. The retry policy is configurable per step — because a browser scraping step and an LLM reasoning step need different retry behavior. 3. State persistence across sessions. If the process crashes entirely — server restart, OOM, network blackout — the workflow state survives. On recovery, it picks up from the last checkpoint, not from scratch. How astron-agent Solves This We built these capabilities into astron-agent — an enterprise-grade agentic workflow platform for building SuperAgents. The core idea: a workflow is not a chain of function calls, it's a stateful process that must survive failures. When you define a multi-step workflow in astron-agent: Each step's input and output are checkpointed Failure at any step triggers isolated retry, not full restart State persists across process restarts and crashes You can resume from any checkpoint, not just the latest one Pair it with astron-rpa for the execution layer — browser automation, desktop operations, form filling. astron-agent handles orchestration and recovery; astron-rpa handles the actual doing. The Pattern Across Today's Trending Look at daily_stock_analysis: it's a multi-step pipeline (collect → analyze → dashboard → push) that runs on a schedule. If any step fails mid-run, the user gets a broken or incomplete result. The project is popular because it solves a real need — but the long-running reliability problem is still on the user to handle. Look at agent-browser: it gives agents browser control, which is a single capability. But when that capability is part of a longer workflow (scrape → process → decide → act), the orchestration challenge appears. The gap between "cool single-step agent demo" and "reliable multi-step agent workflow that runs in production" is exactly this: checkpointing, state persistence, and failure recovery. That's the gap we're filling.

articles.description: When building signup flows, email verification, or notification features, using a personal inbox for every test quickly becomes inconvenient. A temp mail API provides disposable email addresses that developers can use to receive verification messages, extract confirmation links, and test email-based workflows without cluttering their main inbox. SmailPro offers an API for this use case, with temporary Gmail, Outlook, and other email addresses depending on the available plan. It is especially useful for QA, automated testing, staging environments, and privacy-focused prototypes. One important limitation: these mailboxes are designed for receiving emails—not sending or replying—and they should not be used for important or long-term accounts. https://smailpro.com

articles.title: Provider-Assigned IPv6 vs Announcing Your Own Free /48: When to Switch
articles.description: Disclosure up front: I run IPYE, a company that leases IP space. Most of this article is practical how-to; IPYE appears where a free /48, LOA, or ROA helps you try the work, with a short call to action at the end. Every VPS comes with provider-assigned (PA) IPv6, usually a /64 and sometimes a /56. It costs nothing extra and needs no BGP. For many workloads it is the right choice. But PA addresses belong to the provider, and they stay behind when you leave. This article looks at when it makes sense to switch from PA addresses to announcing your own prefix, such as a free IPv6 /48 from IPYE. Examples use PA 2001:db8:aaaa:1::/64 and your own 2001:db8:100::/48. When PA is fine Stay on PA addresses if most of these are true: You have one server, or a few, at one provider. Clients reach you by DNS name, not by address. Nobody allowlists your addresses in their firewall. You can rebuild at another provider in an afternoon and update DNS. In that situation, your own prefix adds a BGP session to maintain and little benefit. Signs that PA has started to hurt Partners allowlist your addresses. Each change means emails and waiting. Addresses are baked into configs you do not control: client VPN profiles, IoT devices, SPF records at customers. You run services across providers and want them in one consistent range. You have moved providers before and the renumbering was painful. You need more than one /64 and the provider will not give you a larger block. Each of these costs a little every time an address changes. Owning the addresses turns that recurring cost into a one-time setup. What you take on Announcing your own prefix requires: an ASN, or a provider that announces the prefix for you a VPS or server with BGP support an LOA, a ROA and an IRR object monitoring for visibility and hijacks With the free /48, setup is instant, the LOA comes from the IPYE portal, and the ROA and route objects are created automatically. The ASN and the BGP-capable host remain your part. Run both side by side You do not have to switch in one step. A Linux host can hold PA and own addresses at the same time: ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:aaaa:1::10/64 dev eth0 # PA, from the provider ip -6 addr add 2001:db8:100::10/128 dev lo # own prefix Keep SSH and management on the PA address, so a BGP problem never locks you out. Move public services to the own prefix one at a time by adding AAAA records for the new address, then removing the old ones. Source address selection With two global addresses, Linux picks the source for outbound connections using RFC 6724 rules, which usually means the address on the outgoing interface. Partners who allowlist your new addresses will see the PA source unless you set it explicitly: ip -6 route replace default via fe80::1 dev eth0 src 2001:db8:100::10 Applications can also bind to a source address directly. Test with curl -6 https://ifconfig.co from the host, which shows the address the outside world sees. A worked flip Bring up BGP and announce the /48 with no services on it. Confirm visibility in public route collectors and run an external ping to 2001:db8:100::10. Add AAAA records for the new address alongside the PA ones. Ask partners to add the new address to their allowlists. Switch the outbound source. After a quiet period, remove the PA AAAA records. Keep the PA addresses configured as a fallback for some weeks. If the BGP session has trouble, you can put the PA AAAA records back. Moving later Once services live in your own range, changing provider becomes a BGP change rather than a renumbering project, and ASN and region changes in the IPYE dashboard apply automatically. Do this next List every place your current PA addresses appear. If that list is long, claim a free /48 from IPYE and run both side by side. Questions: ipye@turnel.com. About IPYE IPYE (https://ipye.com) leases IPv4, IPv6 and ASN space with instant setup. Your first IPv6 /48 is free for the first year, a real allocation you can announce on your own ASN, with a LOA from the portal and the ROA created automatically. ASN and region changes apply automatically. IPv4 /24 to /22 leases include LOA, ROA and per-/24 rDNS; WHOIS is editable on IPv6 /44 and larger. Locations: Los Angeles, New York, Ashburn, Salt Lake City, London, Amsterdam, Frankfurt. Claim your free /48: https://my.ipye.com/products/ipv6-rental. Questions: ipye@turnel.com. Disclosure: I run IPYE

articles.title: S3-Compatible Object Storage Backups Explained in Python (30-Day US/EU Retention)
articles.description: Short answer: object storage fits per-tenant marketplace backups when buckets stay private, restores use expiring signed links, and retention can operate in whole days; choose a dedicated backup system when immutable history is a compliance requirement. The decisive number is restore throughput, not the idle size of the archive. A nightly database dump that is cheap to retain but painful to retrieve during an incident is a failed backup design. For a marketplace keeping 30 daily snapshots per tenant in US or EU storage, I would separate the flow into four boundaries: produce the dump, transfer it, retain it, and authorize a selected restore. Infrai is a reasonable option at the storage boundary when the same team also wants one key and one bill across its backend services, while keeping the integration on plain HTTP instead of adding another provider SDK. That recommendation has a hard edge. It applies to ordinary recoverable exports, not immutable records. How can a Python app test US/EU S3-compatible storage for private data backups? Start with the restore objective. Record the largest expected snapshot, the minimum acceptable restore rate, the region in which the restore worker runs, and the number of simultaneous tenant recoveries the system must tolerate. I'm not sure any vendor comparison can settle throughput from a feature sheet alone; a timed restore drill with representative encrypted data is what resolves it. Your mileage may vary across regions and network paths. Then price the complete path: stored bytes, write and list requests, and egress during routine drills and a real recovery. “Cheapest” without that request and egress model is marketing arithmetic. Don't put the archive in a public bucket to make recovery easier. Keep it private, mint a short-lived download link only after an operator or tenant passes authorization, and log the snapshot ID, tenant ID, requester, and expiry in the application database. The object key should carry the dimensions the storage API can actually filter. For example, tenant/acme/2026-08-15T020000Z/db.dump.zst lets a prefix listing find one tenant without depending on server-side metadata search. Keep a separate catalog row with checksum, logical snapshot ID, byte count, region, creation time, and restore status. That database row is also the right place to prevent two workers from selecting conflicting writes because this storage surface does not offer conditional If-Match writes. One detail matters more than it looks: a 30-day policy is day-granular. Lifecycle expiry has a one-day minimum, so this design cannot promise deletion at 30 days plus exactly zero hours. Compliance language and user-facing retention text should reflect the actual deletion window. Retention policy belongs to application governance Object storage can hold scheduled database dumps, compressed exports, and restore artifacts. It can also return an expiring signed URL so a restore worker downloads one chosen snapshot without receiving the platform API key. The returned URL is its own credential — never attach the Infrai Authorization header to that request. It does not decide whether the dump is transactionally consistent. It does not verify that the marketplace can rebuild listings, orders, and payouts from the file. Those jobs belong to the database export process and the restore runner. This separation is useful: the producer emits a checksummed artifact, storage preserves private bytes for the retention window, and the restore service validates the checksum before applying anything. Large files sharpen that boundary. A single request is acceptable for a genuinely small export, but multipart upload should be a selection requirement for large snapshots because parts can be transferred independently and failed parts can be retried without restarting the whole object. AWS documents the multipart sequence as initiate, upload parts, and complete. Infrai's storage capability includes multipart operations, but multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, so the application should abort abandoned uploads as an explicit housekeeping task. No shortcuts. Provider comparison after the constraints These options solve different ownership problems. The table deliberately avoids volatile unit prices; collect current quotes for the intended region, object size, request volume, and restore drill frequency before committing. Option Integration boundary Large-file decision When I would choose it Main trade-off Infrai One REST surface covering S3, R2, OSS, and COS vendors Validate multipart throughput with a regional restore drill A small backend team already consolidating several services and wanting one key, one bill, and consistent HTTP conventions No object versioning or object lock; GCS and B2 are outside its vendor coverage Amazon S3 directly AWS account, credentials, billing, and SDK/API Multipart upload is documented directly by AWS The team wants a direct specialist relationship and its own provider-specific controls Another credential, integration, and invoice remain in the operating model Cloudflare R2 directly Cloudflare account and direct API/tooling Benchmark from the application region The team wants R2 specifically and prefers to own that provider boundary Switching providers later remains application work Alibaba Cloud OSS directly Alibaba Cloud account and direct API/tooling Benchmark from the selected US or EU path Existing Alibaba Cloud operations already own storage and access policy Provider-specific operations stay with the application team Backblaze B2 directly Backblaze account and direct integration Confirm the intended upload and restore path directly B2 is an explicit requirement It is not available through Infrai's current storage vendor coverage The catch is the durability control model. Infrai's object storage is not suitable when policy requires WORM retention, object lock, recoverable versions after an overwrite, cross-region automatic replication, or permanent public links. Stick with a dedicated backup platform or a direct specialist offering the required controls in those cases. Browser-direct upload is also a poor fit when the team must self-manage bucket CORS, and static-site or image-hosting workloads should go elsewhere because public/public-read ACL is unavailable. For ordinary private snapshots, the consolidation benefit is concrete rather than cosmetic. The storage handoff uses the same bearer key and billing relationship as other backend capabilities, and its discovery surface publishes request schemas and runnable examples. That reduces credential and SDK sprawl around the boundary; it does not replace restore testing or turn basic retention into immutable backup. A Python API example for signed backup links This Python example uploads one already-produced snapshot to a private bucket and requests a signed restore link. It uses only the object write and presign routes, sets an explicit method, supplies an idempotency key for the write, honors Retry-After on a 429, and surfaces other client errors. The single-request upload keeps the example readable; route large production archives through the documented multipart flow after measuring the part size and concurrency that meet the restore objective. Set INFRAI_API_KEY, BACKUP_BUCKET, BACKUP_FILE, and BACKUP_KEY in the environment. The bucket must already exist and remain private. import hashlib import os import time from pathlib import Path import requests API = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" TOKEN = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"] BUCKET = os.environ["BACKUP_BUCKET"] BACKUP_FILE = Path(os.environ["BACKUP_FILE"]) OBJECT_KEY = os.environ["BACKUP_KEY"] def request_with_backoff(method, url, *, headers, data=None, attempts=5): for attempt in range(attempts): response = requests.request( method=method, url=url, headers=headers, data=data, timeout=120, ) if response.status_code != 429: if not response.ok: raise RuntimeError( f"request failed with {response.status_code}: {response.text}" return response retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After") delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt raise RuntimeError("rate limit persisted after 5 attempts") payload = BACKUP_FILE.read_bytes() digest = hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest() auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"} request_with_backoff( "PUT", f"{API}/storage/object/put/{BUCKET}/{OBJECT_KEY}", headers={ **auth, "Content-Type": "application/octet-stream", "Idempotency-Key": f"backup-{digest}", }, data=payload, presign_response = request_with_backoff( "POST", f"{API}/storage/object/presign/{BUCKET}/{OBJECT_KEY}", headers=auth, print(presign_response.json()) The printed response should be passed to the authorized restore job, which extracts the returned signed URL according to the discovery schema. That restore download must use a fresh request without auth; otherwise the platform credential crosses a boundary where it doesn't belong. In production, stream files rather than loading them entirely into memory, and compare a stored SHA-256 digest before the restore begins. Rollout begins with a restore drill Begin with one noncritical tenant and one region. Upload a realistic snapshot, list it by the tenant prefix, generate a signed link, restore into an isolated environment, and measure total recovery time. Repeat with the largest planned object and concurrent restores before choosing upload-part concurrency or declaring an objective met. Next, enable lifecycle retention and a daily check for abandoned multipart uploads. Keep snapshot catalog deletion separate from object deletion so an audit can distinguish “expired by policy” from “missing unexpectedly.” Finally, alert on a backup that was not created, a checksum mismatch, or a restore drill that exceeds its time budget. Delivery systems taught backend teams this lesson years ago: an accepted handoff is not proof of arrival. If this boundary matches the system — private files, signed restores, day-level retention, and application-owned recovery checks — start with the Infrai storage backup guide. If immutability is the requirement, stop here and select the specialist controls first. References https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.presign https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/ https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/oss/ https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

articles.title: A small detail about JSON.stringify() and undefined
articles.description: I noticed something interesting about JSON.stringify() when dealing with undefined values. Take this object: The output is: {"name":"Alex","active":true} The age property is completely missing. I originally expected it to be something like "age": null, but that's not how it works. When JSON.stringify() encounters an undefined value in an object, it skips that property. But arrays behave differently. Here, undefined becomes null instead of being removed. I guess that makes sense, since removing an array element would change the positions of everything after it. There's also a difference between explicitly setting a property to null and leaving it undefined. // {} // {"name":null} This is worth remembering when sending JSON data to an API. For example: fetch("/api/profile", { method: "PATCH", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" }, body: JSON.stringify(updates) }); The request body won't contain bio at all. Depending on how the API handles partial updates, an omitted field might mean "leave it unchanged", while null could mean "clear this field". Not every API follows that convention, though. Anyway, JSON.stringify() is doing what it's supposed to do. It's just easy to forget that JavaScript objects and JSON don't handle undefined in the same way.

articles.title: Bounding Shutdown Retries By Attempt Count Strands The Transcript
articles.description: By Rokas Remeika. Published 24 October 2026. When a voice agent worker shuts down, the framework gives it a fixed time window before killing the process. If your transcript persistence logic retries based on a maximum attempt count, the combined HTTP timeouts can exceed the shutdown window. The process dies mid-write, losing data that only existed in memory. The fix is to budget retries by wall clock. Give the operation a total time budget, and size it so the budget plus one maximum-length HTTP timeout remains strictly inside the framework's shutdown window. Symptoms Transcripts and end-of-call records go missing for calls that ended normally. The write operation is attempted, but the logs stop mid-attempt with nothing after them. The missing records look like flakiness, happening randomly across healthy instances. The failure gets significantly worse whenever the downstream storage service is slow, which is exactly when the end-of-call record matters most for debugging. What is actually happening When a worker process finishes a call or receives a termination signal, the framework running it initiates a teardown phase. The framework gives your shutdown callback a fixed window to clean up and save state. After that window expires, the framework or the host operating system kills the process entirely. Most persistence paths use standard retry libraries or custom loops that bound retries by attempt count. A network write might be configured to retry three times, with a ten-second HTTP timeout per attempt. This works perfectly during normal operation because the process will live indefinitely to see the attempts conclude. During teardown, the process is living on a fixed timer. A persistence path that bounds its retries by attempt count has a worst case measured in attempts, not seconds. Three attempts at a ten-second HTTP timeout can block for thirty seconds. If your framework gives you a twenty-two second graceful shutdown window, you have an eight-second deficit. The downstream service experiences a latency spike. Your first write attempt takes ten seconds and times out. Your second attempt takes ten seconds and times out. You start the third attempt. Two seconds later, the framework's shutdown timer expires. The process receives a SIGKILL while the write is in flight. The memory containing the final transcript is wiped, and data that existed only in that process is gone forever. The bound on your retry logic is real, but it is denominated in the wrong unit. Attempt counts bound the number of failures, not the time. Shutdown windows bound the time, not the failures. How to confirm it Filter your logs for the worker process ID that handled the lost call, starting from the shutdown signal. Expect to see the persistence attempt begin, followed by a hard stop with no subsequent log lines indicating success or failure. Measure the timestamp gap between the shutdown signal and the final log line of the process. Expect this gap to match your framework's exact graceful shutdown timeout limit, proving the process was forcefully killed. Check the downstream storage service logs for the exact minute the call ended. Expect elevated latency or HTTP gateway timeouts that pushed the write duration past its normal baseline, triggering your retry loop. Compare the recorded wall-clock duration of the shutdown callback directly against the framework window in your call event logs. Expect the duration to reach the framework shutdown window limit without any subsequent log indicating completion. How it works The fix is to budget the teardown persistence by wall clock instead of attempt count. You give the whole operation a total time budget, give each attempt its own HTTP timeout, and size them so that the budget plus one maximum-duration in-flight attempt still lands safely inside the shutdown window. Here is the sizing I run in production. The framework provides a 22-second shutdown await window. I give the end-of-call record write an 8-second total wall-clock budget. I give the HTTP client a 10-second per-attempt timeout. If the storage backend is struggling, the loop checks the wall clock. As long as the elapsed time is under 8 seconds, it fires another HTTP request. The worst-case scenario is an attempt starting right before the 8-second budget expires. That final attempt is allowed to block for its full 10-second timeout. The total time elapsed before the HTTP client times out and returns control to the loop is just under 18 seconds. That 18-second worst case fits cleanly against the 22-second shutdown await the framework gives me. The process has time to observe the final failure, log it cleanly, and exit on its own terms before the operating system brings the hammer down. The three numbers in that example are not the transferable part. The inequality is the transferable part: (total_budget + per_attempt_timeout) < framework_shutdown_window. You must write that exact arithmetic in a comment next to the constants in your code. The constraint is completely invisible from any one constant on its own. The next person to review the code will see an 8-second budget, decide it is too tight for a slow backend, raise it, and unknowingly break the system. They will not know what they broke because the increased budget still looks smaller than the 22-second shutdown window on its own. They will only find out when transcripts start vanishing again. What I would check first Check if the session was ended by a function tool calling a teardown routine rather than a normal caller hangup. A tool tearing down the session immediately can cut off final audio and disrupt the lifecycle sequence; if this is the case, arming a pending closure fixes it, as detailed in /blog/voice-agent-end-call-tool-truncates-the-final-sentence-or-loses-the-callers-last/. Check the HTTP response codes returned by the downstream API just before the data loss. An HTTP 400 Bad Request indicates a malformed payload that failed instantly, ruling out timeout starvation. If the downstream storage service returned an HTTP gateway error, the request completed over the network rather than being terminated mid-flight. Check whether the worker process suffered an unexpected crash or host termination prior to the shutdown callback running. Check process supervisor logs to verify whether the process ran until the framework graceful shutdown timer expired. Instrumenting the teardown path Fixing the timeouts stops the data loss, but you need instrumentation to prove the fix holds over time. A teardown sequence is invisible to standard request tracing because the client has already disconnected. I record the shutdown callback wall-clock duration per call and emit it as a structured log event. This allows me to query the duration and compare it against the framework's window across the entire fleet. If the persistence operation starts creeping closer to the 18-second worst case, I can see the degradation before it starts dropping records. Additionally, give an incomplete transcript write its own named failure code on the call's end event. Do not let it land as a generic internal error. When a failure code specifically names the persistence timeout on the end event, you isolate a wall-clock write failure immediately instead of investigating it as a generic error. Generalizing the pattern This failure mode generalises to every teardown path that performs a network write. Whether you are flushing metrics, saving an LLM context window, or writing billing records, the dynamics are identical. Anything you write at teardown that exists nowhere else in the system needs a wall-clock budget derived directly from the window you were given. Common questions Why do my agent transcripts randomly go missing on call end? Your persistence logic is likely taking longer than the graceful shutdown window provided by the framework. When the retry loop exceeds this timer, the process is forcefully killed, and the in-memory transcript is destroyed before it can be saved. How long do I have in a shutdown hook before SIGKILL? It depends entirely on your framework or container orchestrator. You must check the specific graceful shutdown timeout configured in your environment. Should I use a background queue for transcript persistence? Offloading persistence to a separate queue still requires a network write before the worker process is killed. However, you still have to successfully write the payload to the queue during the shutdown window, so the wall-clock constraint applies to the queue publisher as well. Why does setting my HTTP retry count lower not fix the issue? A low attempt count still relies on the per-attempt HTTP timeout. If a single HTTP timeout can exceed the framework shutdown window, lowering the attempt count still leaves the write vulnerable to being killed mid-flight. Canonical URL: https://www.dreamchasers.lt/blog/bounding-shutdown-retries-by-attempt-count-strands-the-transcript

articles.title: One Request, One Deadline: Inside RocketMQ-Rust's Timeout Handling
articles.description: A producer times out while sending a message. Did the request spend its entire budget waiting in a local queue? Did writing to the socket stall? Or did the Broker accept it while the response arrived too late? Those cases need different debugging and retry decisions. RocketMQ-Rust's transport code makes the distinctions worth studying: it carries one deadline through a request, records where an operation stopped, and scopes response correlation to a connection generation. RocketMQ-Rust is an independent community implementation of the RocketMQ messaging system in Rust, not an official Apache Software Foundation release. This walkthrough examines commit ed1c961, inspected on November 9, 2026. It describes that source snapshot rather than announcing a new release. 1. Give the request one clock Imagine a request with a 100 ms budget. It spends 40 ms before reaching the next stage. That stage should have at most 60 ms left. Giving every stage a fresh 100 ms timeout quietly changes the contract. Queueing, writing, and awaiting a response could each consume a full budget. A caller that asked for a bounded operation would experience a much longer wait. The RequestDeadline implementation stores an absolute Tokio instant. Its timeout helper uses tokio::time::timeout_at; copying the deadline preserves the expiry. Asking for the remaining duration saturates at zero, and applying a cap can shorten the deadline without extending it. A simplified timeline looks like this: request entry expiry |-----------------------------------| 0 ms 100 ms | 40 ms elapsed 60 ms remains These numbers illustrate the budget, not measured performance. Deadline accounting also does not turn an asynchronous runtime into a hard real-time system. In Client::send_read, the same deadline travels through pending-response registration, outbound enqueueing, and waiting for the response. The method checks expiry before and after request signing, too. 2. Ask whether writing had started Queueing a request and sending it are separate events. The client registers the pending response before enqueueing the command. If its wait expires while the writer has not started, cancel_before_start() can withdraw that queued work. The method reports a deadline rejection at BeforeWrite. If the work can no longer be withdrawn at that boundary, the timeout path records AwaitingResponse and expires the pending request with a response-timeout error. That label does not prove the Broker processed the message. It tells us that this path cannot establish a clean before-write rejection. This distinction is useful when handling errors: Before-write deadline rejection: this attempt was stopped before its write started. Write failure or timeout: inspect the transport outcome and stage; a generic error alone does not establish remote state. Response timeout: the caller lacks a response, so the Broker-side outcome may be unknown. The project's delivery and retry guide explains why the last case matters. The Broker may already have stored a message when the producer times out. A retry can therefore produce another delivery. Use a stable business event identity across retries. Where repeated processing would be harmful, record the deduplication identity and the business effect atomically. A transport request identifier is not a substitute for that application-level invariant. 3. Bound retained work as well as waiting time A deadline bounds how long a caller should wait. Admission control addresses how much work the transport retains. The pending-request table checks expiry and owner state before acquiring resource budget. Capacity rejection becomes QueueSaturated. Its retained-byte estimate includes command metadata as well as the body, so a header-heavy request is included in byte accounting. This provides another debugging clue: saturation is different from an unresponsive peer. Increasing the timeout does not create capacity. Under pressure, longer waits can keep more pending work around, so measure queueing and retained work alongside latency. 4. Match responses to the connection generation RocketMQ remoting commands use an opaque identifier to correlate a response with a request. Reusing a numeric identifier requires care when old responses can still arrive. RocketMQ-Rust's pending key contains both owner_id and opaque. A PendingRequestOwner represents a physical connection's correlation generation. Once retired by close or timeout, that owner cannot admit more requests; a replacement connection needs a new owner. The scenario is easier to follow with a concrete identifier: Connection generation A registers request 29. The request expires and A is retired. Replacement generation B registers its own request 29. A late response associated with A must not complete B's request. The response associated with B can complete B's request. A targeted unit test exercises this sequence. There is also a useful diagnostic distinction. A response with no matching pending key is classified as Late. An owner from another pending table produces ForeignOwner. The client reader logs the former at debug level and the latter at warning level. Late arrival after timeout or cancellation is an expected possibility. These are local request-correlation guarantees. They do not establish exactly-once message delivery or exactly-once business processing. 5. Test the failure boundary The most instructive part of the deadline integration tests is how they create specific failures: Advance paused Tokio time by 40 ms and check that a 100 ms deadline has 60 ms left. Expire a request before sending and check that the peer-side counter remains zero. Try writing a 1 MiB request through a 64-byte duplex stream to exercise a blocked write. Fill outbound admission and check that rejection does not extend the deadline. Let a loopback peer read a request while withholding its response. The tests separate queue expiry, socket pressure, admission rejection, and absent responses. That makes a failure easier to interpret than one broad assertion that a call “eventually timed out.” To inspect and run the deadline suite at the same snapshot: git clone https://github.com/mxsm/rocketmq-rust.git cd rocketmq-rust git checkout ed1c961748b32fddbe3f416801e4f85491fd6dbc cargo test -p rocketmq-transport --features test-support --test end_to_end_deadline Use the repository's pinned toolchain and build prerequisites. The test source was reviewed for this article; these commands were not executed, and no benchmark results are claimed. Put the distinctions into your runbook When investigating a timed-out send, record the operation stage, admission outcome, total budget, and whether the response was missing after writing could have started. Keep transport retries and application retries within a deliberate overall limit. Then ask the business question separately: if this event arrives again, can the application safely recognize and handle it? RocketMQ-Rust offers a concrete source-level example of keeping those responsibilities separate. One deadline preserves the time budget. Admission bounds retained requests. Connection generations keep late responses attached to the right request history. Application idempotency handles the uncertainty that remains across the network. AI disclosure: This article was drafted and checked by an AI assistant against the linked source code and project documentation. No runtime tests or benchmarks were performed for this article.

articles.title: What broke when I started running ten Claude Code sessions at once
articles.description: I've spent the last few months running five to ten Claude Code sessions at the same time: one session per issue, across a handful of my own projects. Claude Code wrote almost all of the code behind what follows. The bottleneck stopped being the model quite early. It was me. Here's what broke, in order of how much it hurt, and what I changed. 1. I was the message bus Agent A finds something agent B needs. Without help, the only path between them is me copying and pasting. With ten sessions that's most of my day. What I changed: a mailbox per project. A message waits there even when no session is open. An agent reads it with a tool call in the middle of its work, so reading mail doesn't cost a new turn. Urgent messages can wake an idle session; everything else waits until the agent checks. Lesson: most messages between agents aren't urgent. If every message starts a turn, you pay for interruptions nobody needed. 2. Every morning I re-explained the project A fresh session knows nothing. I was writing the same onboarding paragraph again and again. What I changed: a shared memory the agents search before they start digging, and an issue board they pick up, work and close themselves. One tab = one issue, and the tab closes when the issue does. Lesson: "one tab, one issue" did more for focus than any prompt. When a session carries three topics, it mixes them up. 3. Long sessions get expensive, and worse I measured my own sessions. Past roughly 20–25 % of the context window, starting a fresh session with a written handoff was cheaper than carrying on. At 40 % it cost about 28 % more for the same work. What I changed: the agent writes its own handoff (state, decisions, what's next) and a new tab takes over. Lesson: a good handoff is a document a stranger could act on. If it says "as discussed", it isn't one. 4. "All tests pass" isn't always true Agents report green when it isn't: a suite that never ran, a failing check turned off, a test skipped. What I changed: a CI check that ties every commit to its issue and doesn't take the agent's word for the result. Lesson: trust the log, not the summary. 5. I couldn't tell who needed me With ten tabs, the one waiting on my answer looks exactly like the nine that are busy. What I changed: tabs that show who's working, who's finished and who's waiting on me. The app All of this lives in a desktop app for Windows. It's free and runs locally: Claude Code, Codex and OpenRouter sessions side by side. It's in the Microsoft Store as Axon Terminal while we rename it to Lichen: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9P5DW739TTN1 The shared memory, the board and the mailbox need a server, so they'll be a paid account. That part isn't open yet; there's a waitlist at https://uselichen.com/?utm_source=devto How are you handling many agent sessions at once? I'm especially curious how others do handoffs.

articles.title: Mechanics Behind Interactive AI Chat Interfaces: Managing Prompt History and UI Responsiveness
articles.description: You’ve just typed a new message in your favorite AI chat app and hit enter. Within seconds, the AI starts streaming its reply , word by word, sometimes sentence by sentence , while you’re already typing your next question. It feels smooth, responsive, and natural. But have you ever wondered what’s really going on under the hood to make that happen? Managing an ever-growing prompt history, updating the UI incrementally as the AI streams responses, and keeping your input box alive and snappy during heavy async chatter is no small feat. I recently dug into a few popular open-source AI chat frontends and built some prototypes myself. Let me walk you through the key mechanisms that make these interactive AI chat interfaces work so well, especially when juggling prompt history and streaming responses without freezing the UI. The Familiar Developer Headache: UI Freezes and Input Lags During Streaming Imagine this: you hit send and the AI starts streaming a long reply. But your input box feels sluggish, keystrokes lag, or the whole page briefly freezes whenever a chunk of new tokens arrives. You might think this is just network latency or your machine being slow. But the real culprit often lies in how the app manages prompt history, processes incoming tokens, and updates the UI. Many naive implementations update the entire chat transcript state on each token or batch of tokens received. If the prompt history is large, this means copying or re-rendering a huge amount of data very frequently , and that blocks the main thread. The UI stalls, typing feels delayed, and the smooth chat experience breaks down. How Prompt History Management Affects Responsiveness Every message you send and receive typically gets stored in a prompt history array or similar structure. This history is sent along with each new user message to provide context to the AI. When a new message arrives from the AI streaming endpoint, a common approach is to append the incoming partial content to the last assistant message in the history, then update the app's state. But if you naively replace the entire promptHistory array or deeply clone it on every token, you pay a high performance cost. The UI framework tries to re-render large lists, diff long arrays, or reconcile many components repeatedly. This is especially painful in frameworks like React where each state update triggers a render pass. Incremental UI Updates: Appending Tokens Without Rebuilding Everything A better approach is to treat the last assistant message’s content as mutable during streaming. Instead of replacing the entire prompt history, you update only the last item’s content incrementally. This way, you avoid cloning or replacing the entire array on every token. The UI update targets just the message component rendering the assistant’s response. Frameworks with fine-grained reactivity or virtualized lists benefit immensely. Streaming Response Handling: Using Async Iterators and Partial Renders Most AI chat APIs send responses as streamed chunks. The frontend consumes these using async iterators or event streams. for await (const chunk of responseStream) { onNewToken(chunk.text); } Under the hood, the UI updates as tokens arrive, maintaining a fluid typing effect. Some apps batch tokens for every 20-50 characters to reduce update frequency, striking a balance between responsiveness and rendering cost. Keeping Input Responsive: Avoiding Main Thread Blocking Besides prompt history and UI updates, the input box responsiveness is a big challenge. Heavy state updates or layout recalculations triggered by frequent streaming UI changes can block input event handling. Here are a few practical tricks to keep your input responsive: Use requestAnimationFrame or idle callbacks: Schedule UI updates during browser idle time to avoid jank. Debounce or throttle rendering: Don’t update on every token; batch updates. Use Web Workers or off-main-thread processing: Parse and process streaming data off the main thread if possible. Virtualize long chat histories: Don’t render all past messages at once. Example: Incremental Rendering in React In React, you might use a state hook for prompt history. But updating the entire history on every token is costly. Instead, keep the last assistant message content in a separate state: const [messages, setMessages] = useState(initialMessages); // prompt history const [currentResponse, setCurrentResponse] = useState(''); return ( <> {messages.map(m => <Message key={m.id} content={m.content} />)} {currentResponse && <Message content={currentResponse} isStreaming />} <InputBox disabled={isStreaming} /> </> ); This way, the UI updates only the streaming message separately, avoiding large re-renders. Beware of Memory and State Bloat As your conversation grows, so does prompt history size. Sending hundreds of messages each time to the AI can bloat payloads and slow down everything. Common strategies include: Trimming history: Keep only recent or relevant messages. Summarization: Replace older messages with summarized content. Indexed references: Store some context on the server side to avoid resending everything. Managing prompt history efficiently is crucial to keep UI updates fast and smooth. Final Thoughts Creating a smooth, responsive AI chat interface isn’t just about calling an API and rendering text. It’s about carefully managing prompt history data structures, incremental UI updates during streaming, and keeping input responsiveness despite heavy async activity. If you’ve ever debugged a sluggish AI chat frontend, you know the pain of UI freezes and laggy typing. Now you have a better sense of the practical mechanisms under the hood. Next time you build or debug such an interface, watch out for unnecessary array cloning, excessive renders, and blocking state updates. Incremental content updates, careful state partitioning, and batching can make all the difference. Happy coding your next smooth AI chat experience! Helpful learning resources MDN Web Docs web.dev performance guidance React documentation Originally published at Under The Hood. Get the next deep dive in your inbox: subscribe to Under The Hood.

articles.title: Why I Still Write Long-Form in a Short-Video World
articles.description: I run more than fifteen YouTube channels. My audience across Instagram, TikTok and the rest is over ten million people. Short video is where most of those people first meet me. And yet, every week, I sit down and write long-form articles — and I have written six books. People ask me why. The honest answer is that the short clip and the long piece do two different jobs, and I need both. A short video can start a conversation. It cannot finish one. When I started out, I had no capital and no connections. What I had was a skill I could offer and the ability to explain it clearly. That is how I built everything that came after: serving clients through findservicenest.com, founding Buzz Capitol, an independent digital news and media site, and starting Digi Skill Pro Academy, where I now teach free online earning classes to more than ten thousand students. None of that was built on a viral moment. It was built on people understanding what I do, and understanding takes more than sixty seconds. That is the first reason I write long-form: depth is a form of respect. A student who joins one of my free classes is trusting me with their time. A reader of Buzz Capitol is trusting me with their attention. A short clip can promise something; a long piece has to deliver it. When I write about an idea, I have to think it through properly first. I have to decide what I actually believe, in what order, and where the gaps are. Writing is how I find those gaps before my audience does. The second reason is that writing is my thinking tool. I wrote six books — The Silent Disconnect, The Digital Empire, Echoes of Truth, The Resilient Mindset, Beyond the 9 to 5 and Behind the Headlines — while running companies at the same time. I did not write them because I had spare time. I wrote them because running a news site, an academy and a service business produces more questions than answers, and writing is where I work the questions out. A video can show you what I did. An article shows you how I thought about it. Those are not the same thing, and the second one is the part people actually need when they are trying to do something similar themselves. The third reason is about the reader, not me. Some people learn best from a video. Others need to read something slowly, go back over a paragraph, and sit with an idea before they act on it. My academy students come from all kinds of backgrounds, and many of them are starting from zero, just as I did. A long article gives them something they can return to. A clip disappears the moment it ends. A page stays open on their phone. They can re-read it at night, share it with a friend, or work through it step by step. That staying power matters to me more than reach numbers ever will. There is a fourth reason, and it is the one I think about most at Buzz Capitol. I am the founder, CEO and Editor-in-Chief of an independent news site. My job there is to check a story before I publish it, to read past the headline, and to correct something openly when I get it wrong. That is slow work. It is the opposite of what short video rewards. Short video rewards speed and certainty. Long-form rewards patience and doubt. If I only ever made short videos, I would be training myself to be certain about things I have not checked. Writing long-form keeps me honest. It forces me to slow down, verify what I am saying, and say plainly where I am unsure. None of this is an argument against short video. I make it every day, and I will keep making it. Short video is how most people discover anything now, and I am grateful for what it has given me. But discovery is not the same as understanding. A clip can bring someone to my work. Only something longer can show them what the work actually is. So I write. Not because long-form is fashionable — it is not — but because some ideas need room, some readers need depth, and some lessons cannot be shortened without losing the part that matters. The world does not need more content. It needs more of the right kind of content, and that is a decision I make one article at a time.

articles.title: Unit testing RPG with iRPGUnit: what to test, what a failure looks like, and how to run it in CI
articles.description: Most RPG code I have seen is tested the same way: compile, call the program with a few records, look at the report or the screen, and compare by eye. That works until someone changes a rule six months later and nobody remembers which records proved it. iRPGUnit gives RPG the same kind of unit tests other languages have had for years. This article shows a real suite of 20 tests, what the report looks like when everything passes, and, more useful, what it looks like when something is wrong. Everything below was run on PUB400 (IBM i 7.5, iRPGUnit v6.0.5) and the output is copied from those runs. First, something you can test A unit test calls a procedure with known input and checks the result. That only works if the rule lives in a procedure that does not read a file, write a record or show a screen. In legacy code that is rarely the case. In my modernization showcase the payment rules of an accounts receivable application were buried in the calculation specs of two programs, between CHAINs and indicators. Step 3 of the modernization moved them into a service program, ARSRV, with six small procedures and no I/O: dcl-proc AR_ageBucket export; dcl-pi *n int(10); daysPastDue int(10) const; end-pi; select; when daysPastDue <= 0; return AR_BUCKET_CURRENT; when daysPastDue <= 30; return AR_BUCKET_1_30; when daysPastDue <= 60; return AR_BUCKET_31_60; when daysPastDue <= 90; return AR_BUCKET_61_90; other; return AR_BUCKET_OVER_90; endsl; end-proc; The programs that read the files now call these procedures. The tests call them too, without any files at all. This is the part that takes the real work. Writing the tests afterwards is quick. What a test suite looks like An iRPGUnit test suite is a NOMAIN module. Every exported procedure whose name starts with test is one test case. You include the iRPGUnit prototypes and the prototypes of the code under test: **FREE ctl-opt nomain option(*srcstmt:*nodebugio); /copy RPGUNIT/QINCLUDE,TESTCASE /copy QRPGLESRC,ARSRVPR dcl-proc test_validate_amount_checked_first export; aEqual(AR_MSG_INVALID_AMOUNT : AR_validatePayment(0 : *off)); dcl-proc test_days_over_leap_day export; iEqual(2 : AR_daysPastDue(d'2024-03-01' : 20240228)); dcl-proc test_bucket_boundaries export; iEqual(AR_BUCKET_CURRENT : AR_ageBucket(-19)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_CURRENT : AR_ageBucket(0)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_1_30 : AR_ageBucket(1)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_1_30 : AR_ageBucket(30)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_31_60 : AR_ageBucket(31)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_31_60 : AR_ageBucket(60)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_61_90 : AR_ageBucket(61)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_61_90 : AR_ageBucket(90)); iEqual(AR_BUCKET_OVER_90 : AR_ageBucket(91)); (Replace RPGUNIT with the library where iRPGUnit is installed.) Two commands do the rest: RUCRTRPG TSTPGM(ARSRVT) SRCFILE(QRPGLESRC) BNDSRVPGM(ARSRV) RUCALLTST TSTPGM(ARSRVT) DETAIL(*ALL) RUCRTRPG compiles the module and creates the test service program bound to the code under test. RUCALLTST runs every test procedure and writes a spooled file named RPGUNIT. The full suite has 20 test cases: every validation rule, every bucket boundary (0/1, 30/31, 60/61, 90/91), a leap day, a payment larger than the invoice, and one test for a defect the legacy program really had (more on that below). The last line of the report: Success. 20 test cases, 28 assertions, 0 failure, 0 error. What a failure looks like A green report proves less than it seems. The useful question is: if someone breaks a rule, does a test notice? So I made a copy of the service program, ARSRVX, with one character changed: when daysPastDue < 30; // DELIBERATE DEFECT: should be <= 30 An invoice exactly 30 days overdue now lands in the 31-60 bucket. On a real aging report that moves money from one column to the next, and the totals still add up, so nobody sees it. I bound the same, unchanged test suite to the broken copy and ran it: TEST_BUCKET_BOUNDARIES - FAILURE Expected 2, but was 3. TEST_BUCKET_BOUNDARIES (ARSRVTX->ARSRVTX:9400) Expected: 1 '2' Actual: 1 '3' ----------------------- ... FAILURE. 20 test cases, 23 assertions, 1 failure, 0 error. Three things in this report are worth knowing: It points at the line. 9400 is the source statement (94.00, thanks to option(*srcstmt)) of the assertion that failed: iEqual(AR_BUCKET_1_30 : AR_ageBucket(30)). A failed assertion ends the test case. The suite had 28 assertions when it passed, and only 23 ran this time. The boundary test stopped at its fourth assertion, so the five after it never ran. If one test checks many things, you only learn about the first one that is wrong. That is a reason to keep test cases small, or at least to put the cheapest checks first. The other 19 tests stayed green. The failure names the rule that broke, not just "something changed". Failure, error, and an exception you expect iRPGUnit separates two kinds of red. To see both, I wrote a small demo suite (RUDEMOT) with one of each: dcl-proc test_failure_on_purpose export; aEqual('A' : AR_customerStatus('H' : 0.01) : 'status'); dcl-proc test_error_on_purpose export; dcl-s zero int(10) inz(0); dcl-s x int(10); x = 100 / zero; The report: TEST_ERROR_ON_PURPOSE - ERROR MCH1211 - Attempt made to divide by zero for fixed point operation. TEST_ERROR_ON_PURPOSE (RUDEMOT->RUDEMOT:6100) TEST_FAILURE_ON_PURPOSE - FAILURE status: Expected 'A', but was 'H'. TEST_FAILURE_ON_PURPOSE (RUDEMOT->RUDEMOT:5300) Expected: 1 'A' Actual: 1 'H' A failure means the code ran and returned the wrong answer. An error means the code crashed. The third parameter of aEqual ('status') is a field name that is put in front of the message. With several assertions in one test it tells you which value was wrong without opening the source. Sometimes the exception is the expected result. What does AR_daysPastDue do with a due date of 2026-13-32 from bad data? It should not return a number. You can test that with monitor and getMonitoredMessage: dcl-proc test_bad_due_date_is_an_exception export; dcl-ds msg likeds(MsgInfo_t); dcl-s days int(10); monitor; days = AR_daysPastDue(d'2026-10-31' : 20261332); fail('AR_daysPastDue accepted 2026-13-32'); on-error; msg = getMonitoredMessage(*on); endmon; aEqual('RNX0112' : msg.id); This test passed: the procedure ends with RNX0112 (date, time or timestamp value is not valid). If someone later "fixes" the procedure so it quietly returns 0 for a bad date, the fail() line turns this test red, and the team has to decide on purpose whether that is the behavior they want. setUp, tearDown, and the order tests run in iRPGUnit calls four optional procedures if you export them: setUpSuite and tearDownSuite once around the whole suite, and setUp and tearDown around every test. They are the place to create test data, clear a work file, or reset a data area. I wanted to see the exact order, so each procedure in the demo suite appended one word to a data area. In the source, the tests are written in this order: numeric, failure, error, baddate. The data area after the run: setUpSuite setUp baddate tearDown setUp error tearDown setUp failure tearDown setUp numeric tearDown tearDownSuite Two things: tearDown ran after the failed test and after the crashed test too. Cleanup in tearDown is safe even when a test goes wrong. In the failing test, the line after the failed aEqual never ran (there is no after-failed-assert in the trace). The tests ran in alphabetical order of their names, not in source order. The report is sorted the same way. Do not write a test that depends on another test having run first. If two tests need the same data, create it in setUp. Small things that cost me time Comparing numbers as strings. One of my first tests was: aEqual('.00' : %char(AR_applyAmount(0 : 500.00))); // %char drops the leading zero It passes, but only because I wrote '.00' after seeing what %char returns. iRPGUnit 6 (the version on PUB400) also has an overloaded assertEqual that compares numbers as numbers, which says what you mean. Both lines below passed in the demo suite: assertEqual(0 : AR_applyAmount(0 : 500.00)); assertEqual(300.00 : AR_applyAmount(300.00 : 500.00)); Testing the bug you fixed. The legacy report program printed *UNKNOWN* (FICTIONAL) for a missing customer, because a MOVEL of *UNKNOWN* left the end of the previous customer's name in the field. The fix is one line. The test that keeps it fixed is just as short: dcl-proc test_unknown_customer_has_no_leftover_name export; aEqual('*UNKNOWN*' : %trimr(AR_customerName(*off : 'EKA FOODS (FICTIONAL)'))); Every defect you fix is a test case you already know you need. Running the tests in CI RUCALLTST ends with escape message CPF9897 when any test fails or errors (FAILURE. 20 test cases, 23 assertions, 1 failure, 0 error.). Called through the system command in PASE, that is a non-zero exit code, which is all a CI pipeline needs. In my ibmi-inventory project, a GitHub Actions job builds the code from Git with IBM Bob (makei) and then runs this over SSH on the IBM i: system "$RULIB/RUCRTRPG TSTPGM($OBJLIB/DATEUTILT) SRCSTMF('$PWD/qrpglesrc/dateutilt.rpgle') BNDSRVPGM(($OBJLIB/DATEUTIL)) TGTCCSID(*JOB)" system "$RULIB/RUCALLTST TSTPGM($OBJLIB/DATEUTILT) DETAIL(*ALL)" 2>&1 | tee .logs/rpgunit.txt grep -q "Success" .logs/rpgunit.txt The script runs with set -euo pipefail, so the escape message from a failed run stops it even though the output goes through tee (without pipefail, the exit code of that line would be tee's, and a red test would pass the pipeline). The last grep is a second check: the job is green only if the report really says Success. The report goes into the job's artifacts, so the reviewer of a pull request sees which test went red without signing on to the IBM i. The rules I follow Move the rule out of the I/O first. A procedure with no files is easy to test. A program full of CHAINs is not. Test the boundaries, not the middle. 0, 1, 30, 31. The off-by-one in this article was caught only by the test for exactly 30. Break the code on purpose once. If no test goes red, the suite proves less than it seems. Keep test cases small. A failed assertion ends the test, so the checks after it tell you nothing. Never depend on test order. Shared data goes in setUp, cleanup in tearDown. Every fixed defect gets a test. It is the cheapest test to write and the one most likely to matter again. Let the pipeline run them. Tests that need a person to remember to run them stop being run. The full suite, the service program and the regression outputs are in the modernization showcase repository. If your shop runs RPG unit tests in a pipeline, I would like to hear how you handle tests that need database data: a test library per run, setUp with SQL inserts, or something else.

articles.title: A $1.50 search API where the URL is the interface
articles.description: I use a hosted Google search API to find company websites from a company name, and I switched to Bright Data's SERP endpoint because the billing model fits intermittent use: $1.50 per 1,000 successful requests, a 5,000 request monthly free tier, no monthly minimum, and failed requests are not billed. Then my first accuracy test confirmed 15 of 25. The API was not slow and it was not erroring. Two parameters were missing from the URL I sent, and one of them changed the search results from Japan to India. The call The endpoint takes a search URL and returns the engine's response. For Google with organic results in a light JSON shape: curl -X POST https://api.brightdata.com/request \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $BRIGHTDATA_TOKEN" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "zone": "", "format": "raw", "url": "https://www.google.com/search?q=ACME+%E6%A0%AA%E5%BC%8F%E4%BC%9A%E7%A4%BE&hl=ja&gl=jp&brd_json=parsed_light", "data_format": "parsed_light" }' format: "raw" returns the body as text. brd_json=parsed_light asks for the parsed view, and data_format tells the API to hand it back as JSON rather than a string. The five things that broke Symptom Cause Fix Japanese companies missing from results no gl parameter, so the geolocation defaulted elsewhere set gl=jp (and hl=ja) 400 with no useful message num is rejected by the SERP layer ask for the default page size, paginate with start if needed request timed out brd_json=1 (full JSON) on a heavy result set use brd_json=parsed_light took 6 to 12 seconds per call it is a real browser fetch, not a cached index budget for it, run calls concurrently occasional 502 upstream fetch failure retry once, then treat as no result The geolocation one is the expensive mistake. With no gl, the API returned results with a country field of India or Portugal for Japanese company names. Nothing in the response says the search was performed from the wrong place; the results just look plausible and are wrong. If your pipeline extracts the first organic link, you get a confident wrong answer. What the numbers looked like I test any search provider against a hard set: 25 companies whose websites I have already confirmed by hand, chosen because name-based guessing had failed on them before. For each company I count three things separately: retrieved: the correct domain appears anywhere in the organic results confirmed: my verification step accepts it as the company's site false confirmation: the pipeline accepted a wrong domain Path Retrieved Confirmed Wrong domain accepted guessed URL from the company name, old rules not applicable 15 of 25 yes, before a Japan check was added plain JSON, no geolocation 16 of 25 0 parsed light JSON with gl=jp 19 of 25 Retrieval went from 64 percent to 76 percent just by telling the API where I was searching from. The confirmed count moved more, because correct results that were previously outranked by same-name foreign companies became reachable. Zero wrong domains in the two API configurations is the number I care about most, and it is zero because the verification step now requires evidence that the page belongs to a Japanese entity: Japanese text, a Japan address, or a location. Before that check existed, the guessing path nearly accepted a Slovenian domain for a Japanese company whose name matched. For this use case a miss costs one manual lookup, and a wrong domain corrupts the record silently. What comes back parsed_light gives you the organic block as structured JSON: position, title, link, description, plus the engine's own metadata. It is around ten results, which is what the first page holds. The full JSON variant contains every module Google renders on that page, and on a rich result set it is large enough that the whole request occasionally fails. If you need a knowledge panel or related questions, pay for the full parse deliberately rather than by default. One billing detail that surprised me, from the docs: the pay-per-success model applies to the standard configuration. If you set custom headers or cookies on the zone, every request is billed including failures, and retries are still not extra. If you need a specific Accept-Language or a consent cookie, model the cost as "all attempts" rather than "successes". Where this tool is the wrong choice For anything that can wait, a queued batch API is cheaper per request. This endpoint exists for the case where you want the answer in the same second, and you pay for that: a real browser, a proxy that is not your datacenter IP, and a parser on the other side. It is also not a search index. Asking it the same question repeatedly costs the same every time, so caching the query and the result is not optional at any volume. What it costs at different volumes, and where the cheaper option is not the one you would guess, is in the pricing model post. If you have moved a scraping job from a self-hosted headless browser to a hosted SERP API: what did you lose that you did not expect? Originally published at agentjournal.dev.
